newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech crown stronger on govt moves, market nervous.
newsitem.headline: Czech crown stronger on govt moves, market nervous.

text.p: The Czech crown strengthened on Thursday after the government unveiled fresh measures to revive the economy, but some analysts questioned whether the plan could be put into action.

Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus, in a dramatic acknowledgement of the Czech economy's problems, announced on Wednesday sweeping cabinet changes and a six-point recovery plan, including spending cuts and a public sector wage freeze.

"Everything they want to do is great. I just give them about a five percent chance of actually being able to execute it and that is what the market is sceptical about," said Matt Starr, director of capital markets at Creditanstalt in Prague.
The crown firmed against the mark in morning trade to stand at 19.138 to the mark and 32.575 to the dollar at 1130 GMT, compared with 19.306 and 32.737 late on Wednesday.

"The crown reacted positively to the changes in the government and the newly announced plan," said trader Jan Dosek of CSOB. "But people are still afraid to go long in Czech crowns because they expect the central bank to cut official interest rates in the coming week or so," he said.
The government moves followed two turbulent weeks for the currency as investors, alarmed at yawning trade and current account deficits as well as political uncertainty, dumped the crown.

The central bank eventually caved in and, after raising its discount rate to 13 percent from 10.5, allowed the crown to float from Tuesday. It immediately weakened some eight percent before recouping some of this in an illiquid market.
The government package is intended to restore balance to the economy and stabilise the currency.

"One thing is what is written in the programme and another is if the current government will be able to implement it because of its low popularity and consequently bad bargaining position," said economist Jiri Krovak of WoodCommerz.
The fresh spending cuts, put by deputy premier Josef Lux at "tens of billions" of crowns, come on top of 25.5 billion crowns in cuts announced in another austerity package in April.
The cuts will need the approval of parliament where the ruling three-party coalition has the slenderest majority.
The previous package also included public sector wage growth limits and Krovak said it would be difficult to amend wage deals already agreed.
"The contract for this year has already been signed so this will depend on the willingness of the unions to renegotiate," he said.
Czech Federation of Trade Unions leader Richard Falbr said any wage freeze should be accompanied by the scrapping of recently agreed rent and energy price rises.
"If the government wants to put the brakes on wage growth, it should also give up something, above all cancel the deregulations. That is a minimum," he said in the Mlada Fronta Dnes daily.
Several analysts have said they see a further fall in the crown once interest rates come down.
Dosek said it could fall to 20-21 to the mark before coming back to around current levels. Starr said it was only likely to settle after a gradual fall of a further 10-15 percent.
Tomas Becvar of Komercni Banka said the pledge to cut spending and restore balance to the budget were welcome but he also saw interest rates as the key factor for the crown.
"I still see a range of 19-20 (crowns) to the mark.I do not expect any bigger depreciation of the crown in the near term."
